source.title: How much progress have we made in neural network training? A New Evaluation Protocol for Benchmarking Optimizers
source.authors: Yuanhao Xiong; Xuanqing Liu; Li-Cheng Lan; Yang You; Si Si; Cho-Jui Hsieh

record.file_problem: Full paper text is supplied; it includes the paper's appendices and references.
record.tranche_reason: Its optimizer comparisons refine the claim that adaptive optimizers generally generalize worse: the study reports task-dependent outcomes under a tuning protocol that includes hyperparameter search and early stopping. It does not measure train-test generalization gaps directly.
record.gate_note: The paper benchmarks optimizer efficiency and task evaluation performance, not training error, test error, memorization of random labels, or the gap between training and test error. The optimizer results bear on V4's held-out performance component. The human-tuning comparison and data-addition results do not measure any claim version's stated gap or behavior; optimizer values used for benchmarking are retained where they report the claim-relevant held-out performance.
record.test_reason: Table 8 compares held-out peak performance of adaptive optimizers and SGD on image classification and language tasks under limited and broader hyperparameter tuning. This tests V4 through a different benchmarking protocol. Training-performance comparisons are unnecessary for V4's held-out-performance component but would be needed to establish its training-versus-test qualification.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors find no clear overall winner, no consistent improvement over Adam from newer optimizers, competitive image-classification performance including SGD, and generally better adaptive-method performance on NLP, graph, and reinforcement-learning tasks. These conclusions cover both efficiency and peak performance, which should be distinguished.
record.recipe_differences: The study benchmarks several optimizers using a proposed Hyperband-based end-to-end tuning protocol and a data-addition training protocol; it does not reproduce the claim's generalization-gap experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Optimizer rankings change across tasks and with the tuning regime (learning rate only versus every hyperparameter). The paper also reports a slight ranking change after adding data, but that does not directly measure a claim-version generalization gap.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 3 reports early-weighted cumulative held-out performance during hyperparameter search, combining tuning efficiency and model performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer efficiency rankings depend on the task, tuning budget, search strategy, and tunable parameters.

record.problems: No train-test error gaps are reported, so held-out accuracy or task metrics cannot establish optimizer effects on generalization gaps. Table 3 does not show uncertainty or repetition counts; the MRPC table labels accuracy while the surrounding text describes F1.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports other optimizer/task values in Table 3, including CelebA, PPI, and Walker2d-v3, but these are not assigned to V4 because the version's stated image-classification and language benchmarks and standard training/test performance comparison do not cleanly map to all these tasks. Data-addition values in Table 4 and GAN values in Table 9 are also not extracted: these do not report training-versus-test gaps or test V4's limited-tuning comparison.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, chance-level random-label test accuracy, and coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width beyond interpolation and its effect on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Whether adaptive methods have equal or better training performance despite worse held-out performance; decoupled weight decay; switching Adam to SGD; word-level language modeling.
Batch-size comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove their penalty.
Controlled dropout or weight-decay removal comparisons.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples.

missing.what: Peak held-out performance for SGD and Adam: learning-rate-only CIFAR-10 93.39/93.65, CIFAR-100 73.68/71.51, MRPC 71.05/84.90; full tuning CIFAR-10 93.47/92.58, CIFAR-100 73.94/73.82, MRPC 72.80/88.46. Add comparison rows with matched SGD baselines. MRPC's metric is inconsistently identified as accuracy or F1.
missing.locator: Appendix E.1, Table 8; Appendix D for tuning conditions

missing.what: Peak results for the other adaptive optimizers are needed to assess the broader adaptive-method claim. For example, RAdam exceeds SGD on CIFAR-10 under both tuning regimes, whereas all adaptive methods fall below SGD on CIFAR-100 under learning-rate-only tuning.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V4. Verdicts use the supplied text's Table 8 because all extracted rows report CPE. Lack of training-error measurements does not exclude held-out optimizer comparisons from V4. The protocol specifies averaging repetitions, but tables provide neither uncertainty nor an explicit repetition count. Small peak differences should therefore not be interpreted as established statistical differences.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Effect of widening beyond the interpolation threshold on test error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image generalization.

Image and language benchmarks include optimizer comparisons, but the study does not compare training versus test performance or test equal/better training performance. It does not test broad tuning, decoupled weight decay, switching Adam to SGD, or word-level language models.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Effect of dropout and weight decay on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other properties tracking the generalization gap.
Removing memorized examples and resulting test accuracy.

relationships.reason: From Table 8, missing from the rows: Adam remains below SGD, 92.58% versus 93.47%, while RAdam reaches 94.47%; broader tuning does not uniformly favor adaptive methods.

source_check.reason: Table 8 reports Adam 92.58%, SGD 93.47%, and RAdam 94.47%. V4 already says broader tuning can reverse the difference; it does not predict that every adaptive optimizer benefits.
